title: LRU cache
short: Keep the recently used items, drop the stalest one.
what: A cache keeps a few results close at hand so you don't fetch them again. When it is full, an LRU (least recently used) cache throws out the item that was used longest ago. A dict gives one-step lookups, and the dict's order tracks which item is oldest.
analogy: A small desk with room for three books. When you need a fourth, the one you haven't opened for the longest goes back to the shelf.

frames.label: cache
frames.say: An empty cache that holds at most 3 items. The top row will always be the least recently used one.

frames.label: cache
frames.say: put a, b and c. They line up in the order they were used: a is the oldest, c the newest.

frames.label: cache
frames.say: get("a") finds 1 in one step through the dict. Using a counts as a fresh use.

frames.label: cache
frames.say: So a moves to the bottom as the newest. Now b is the least recently used.

frames.label: cache
frames.say: put("d", 4), but the cache is full. Throw out the top row: b, unused for the longest time.

frames.label: cache
frames.say: d goes in at the bottom as the newest. Order now: c, a, d.

frames.label: cache
frames.say: get("b") misses because b was evicted. Every get and put took O(1).

when: Keep only the last N used items
get and put both in O(1)
Evict the least recently used item
watch: Both get and put count as a use. Move the key to the newest end in both.
Evict after inserting, and only when you are over capacity.
Interviews may ask you to build it from a dict plus a doubly linked list instead of OrderedDict.
